title: feat: ChatGPT subscription images via Codex CLI (no API key)
body:
## Что добавлено

Новый режим `draw --provider chatgpt` (`codex` — алиас): генерация через установленный официальный Codex CLI, авторизованный аккаунтом ChatGPT, без отдельного OpenAI API-ключа и без управления ChatGPT Desktop.

```bash
npm install -g @openai/codex@latest
codex login
pipx install --force 'git+https://github.com/alex-mextner/draw-cli@feat/chatgpt-subscription-images'
draw install-skill
draw --provider chatgpt --check
draw 'Кот-космонавт, акварель' --provider chatgpt -o cat.png
```

Hugging Face остаётся default для backward compatibility; `DRAW_PROVIDER=chatgpt` делает подписочный backend default.

## Как работает

README теперь содержит Mermaid-схему полного потока: `draw` → локальная валидация → Codex preflight → fresh temp workspace → `codex exec` через stdin → native `image_gen` → thread-scoped native PNG → проверка regular file/link/size/decode → atomic output replace.

Ключевые гарантии:

- ChatGPT login обязателен; API-key login отвергается.
- API/provider env overrides вырезаются только из child environment.
- Нет автоматического API/HF fallback и нет автоматических generation retries.
- User/project Codex config/rules не наследуются для generation turn; shell/web/apps/multi-agent отключены, shell sandbox read-only.
- Prompt не попадает в shell argv; до 1 MiB UTF-8.
- До 5 reference images, каждая до 32 MiB; native output до 32 MiB.
- Result берётся только из текущего canonical thread UUID или fresh workspace, а не из agent-authored path / глобального newest file.
- Symlink/hardlink/ambiguous/corrupt output отвергается; существующий output меняется атомарно только после полной проверки.

## GPT Image 2.5

[Официальный Images 2.5 rollout](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-images-2-5/) включает Codex, но native Codex image tool не даёт image-model selector; в просмотренном клиентском исходнике по-прежнему есть internal identifier `gpt-image-2`. Поэтому PR не притворяется, что может закрепить Flare/Sunburst через подписку: `draw` использует native image backend, доступный текущему ChatGPT/Codex account rollout.

`--model` — HF-only. `--codex-model` выбирает reasoning model, вызывающую image tool, а не сам image generator.

## Adversarial review + TDD

Проведён отдельный adversarial review с пяти позиций:

1. security / credential & path injection;
2. reliability / filesystem / cancellation / wall clock;
3. CLI & product UX / silently ignored flags;
4. upstream Codex compatibility;
5. resource-abuse / fuzz limits.

Подробный отчёт: `docs/adversarial-review.md`.

RED→GREEN история сохранена в PR. Первый намеренно RED commit:

- `7f7a4bd2b86172fcc02c4d169f2306f5590f0085` — `test(red): add adversarial TDD cases for subscription backend`; GitHub Actions `tests` действительно завершился failure.

Он зафиксировал до исправления:

- local reference validation до запуска Codex;
- prompt-size bound;
- отказ от silently ignored provider-specific flags;
- корректный контракт `--check`;
- artifact lookup без зависимости от wall-clock mtime;
- assignment-style credential redaction.

Второй RED documentation-contract commit:

- `3bff3d094916388df7b2b5e48bd306a4a722ff78` — архитектурная схема, текущие billing/model/limit claims README.

Во время последующих прогонов CI поймал ещё отдельный красный цикл, включая documentation-contract regression; исправления внесены отдельными commits, а не переписаны поверх RED history.

## Тестирование

Добавлены/расширены:

- real-subprocess fake-Codex contract tests;
- adversarial regression tests;
- executable README/documentation contracts;
- Python 3.9 + 3.12 Linux matrix;
- отдельный macOS offline adapter/adversarial/docs job;
- opt-in real `codex` preflight (`DRAW_LIVE_CODEX=1`), без image generation;
- opt-in real generation (`DRAW_LIVE_CODEX_GENERATE=1`), которое может расходовать ChatGPT plan allowance и поэтому никогда не включено в CI.

README также полностью пересмотрен: удалено устаревшее утверждение, что HF read token сам по себе означает бесплатный inference; теперь auth отделён от HF credits/billing. Installer completion text тоже описывает оба backend-а.

## Что намеренно не заявляется

- Нет server-side attestation конкретного Flare/Sunburst checkpoint.
- Локальный официальный `codex` binary считается trusted computing base.
- Убийство локального process group на timeout не отменяет уже отправленный server-side request/usage.
- Native Codex artifacts не удаляются автоматически.

`main` не изменён; PR не слит.

title: feat: terminology dictionary, context comparison, and stt login
body:
Three features that share one theme: the speech model does not know your words, and it does not tell you when it is unsure.

## Terminology — `stt dict`

One five-minute recording produced ConLoca, Conloca, ConLog and ConLoka for a single project name, and "Vigma" for Figma. A dictionary now reaches the run in three places, deliberately:

- **as the speech model's initial prompt** — the only one of the three that can fix a word at the acoustic level. Measured on a real recording: three of four ConLoca mentions came back spelled correctly.
- **as an exact substitution** for spellings the user recorded as wrong (`--aka`). The original wording is kept as a variant, so `--text raw` still returns what was actually said.
- **as a glossary in the LLM correction prompt**, with the phonetic near-misses attached.

The rule that separates the last two: a spelling the user wrote down is a fact and is substituted; a phonetic near-match is a suspicion and is only ever flagged, for the reader and for the correction pass. `stt dict check "<line>"` runs the real screen the pipeline runs, so the command that explains a decision executes that decision rather than an approximation of it.

## Context comparison — `--context`, `--context-compare`

Feeding the decoder its own previous output fixes casing, punctuation and proper nouns across window boundaries, and is also exactly what lets one hallucinated sentence become five minutes of fiction. Rather than choosing for everybody, stt can decode twice and keep the disagreements as variants for the correction pass to weigh, joined by time rather than by index. The loop-safe pass stays primary, so a runaway repetition can never become the transcript.

One caveat, documented in the README where the feature is described: on whisper.cpp a pinned glossary needs a nonzero context budget to have any effect at all, so a run with a dictionary buys itself 64 tokens and the loop-safety guarantee becomes bounded rather than absolute. `--no-dict-bias` keeps `--context off` literal for anyone who prefers the guarantee to the terminology; mlx-whisper pins the prompt for free and is unaffected.

## Credentials — `stt login`, `stt logout`

Speaker diarization needs a Hugging Face token behind two gated models. That used to be a paragraph of instructions with a place to stop at every step. It is now one command that opens the right pages in order, picks the token off the clipboard, verifies it against the API, stores it where `huggingface_hub` itself looks (so every Hugging Face tool on the machine is logged in, which is also why `logout` says out loud that it signs them all out), and checks that each model is genuinely unlocked.

## What the cache had to learn

Everything above changes the words, so all of it had to enter the archive's identity without invalidating the runs already stored: a new setting is hashed only when it is set away from its default, and a drift test pins that table to the real defaults.

The rule the whole change rests on, now written into `AGENTS.md`: **anything that changes the words is settled before the fingerprint is computed.** Whisper.cpp ignores an initial prompt at `-mc 0`, so a carried glossary buys itself a context budget — and that purchase is made in the settling pass, where the cache key can see it, rather than inside the command-line builder where it could not. When an engine cannot do what was asked (an older `whisper-cli` that cannot pin the glossary to every window, an mlx build without the parameter, a `--variant-model` that would not resolve), the shortfall goes into the key, so upgrading is a cache miss rather than a stale answer served forever.

On the ordinary path the archive is consulted before any engine is touched — a transcript made months ago is still that transcript after whisper.cpp is removed or downgraded. Finding one of the narrowed runs does cost the capability probes; that is the price of a key that tells the truth, and it is written down.

## Review

350 tests, `ruff` and `mypy` clean. Thirty-three rounds of multi-model review (Opus, Codex, Fable), which between them turned up:

- three separate ways a hand-edited `dictionary.json` could be silently truncated on the next write — an entry that is not an object, a term made of separators, and an alias written without its brackets. Each loaded as a smaller dictionary, and the next unrelated `stt dict add` saved that smaller version over the file.
- a glossary that reached the decoder on one engine and did nothing at all on another, while both runs were keyed as if it had worked.
- a login that destroyed a working stored token because a revoked `$HF_TOKEN` shadowed it.
- an alias that could silently rename a real product (`dict add Figma --aka Sketch`, then `dict add Sketch`).
- CSV formula injection through an imported glossary, and terminal escape sequences through the same door.
- a captive portal answering 200 to everything being reported as a successful login.

## Known and deliberately left

`stt mic` (live dictation) and Ollama as an LLM provider are not in this change; both are tracked separately, as are three design seams the last review rounds named. `--diarize` has been unblocked by `stt login` but has still not been run end to end on a real recording.

title: feat: `stt mic` — live dictation into whatever window has focus
body:
## What this adds

`stt mic` opens the microphone and types what you say into whatever window has focus,
correcting it underneath you as a better answer arrives. It is the last item from the
original brief that had not been built.

```
stt mic                    # speak; words appear where you are already typing
stt mic --check            # is it hearing you? levels, the bar, and the verdict
stt mic --list-devices     # which microphone is which
stt mic --no-draft         # nothing is typed until it is final
```

Two macOS permissions are needed, both granted to the terminal application rather than to
stt, because that is the level macOS grants them at: **Accessibility**, to type at all, and
**Microphone**, the first time it records. `stt mic --check` reports on both and types
nothing anywhere.

## Two models, not one

`base` answers about the sentence so far in roughly forty milliseconds, so words appear
while they are still being spoken. `large-v3-turbo` answers about the finished sentence one
to three seconds later and replaces them with the version that has the proper nouns, the
capitals and the punctuation right. Your terminology dictionary reaches both, so a project
name is spelled the way you wrote it down.

The two never write at the same time. They decode different audio into the same caret, and
if their answers could arrive in either order the text would assemble itself backwards, so
drafting stops while a sentence settles. Neither model is launched per sentence either:
`whisper-cli` loads its weights on every run, which is longer than the entire latency
budget, so both are held open by `whisper-server` from the same whisper.cpp build.

## It never deletes a character it did not type

Correcting text in place means deleting text, which is safe only while the characters to the
left of the caret are still the ones stt put there. A listen-only event tap reports the
moment a human touches the keyboard, and the answer is to let go of the sentence in flight
entirely — not to tidy it, not to finish it. stt's own synthetic keystrokes come back
through that same tap, so each carries a random per-session marker the watcher ignores.

Ownership is remembered per sentence rather than as a single flag, which review caught and
is worth stating because the flag was wrong in a way that mattered: the user takes over
sentence A, then starts speaking sentence B before A has finished decoding, and beginning B
cleared the flag — so A's answer arrived and was typed, text the user had explicitly
rejected, at whatever caret they had moved to by then, possibly in a different application.
A sentence taken over is now never typed and never appears in the printed transcript either,
so what is printed at the end is what went into the window.

A system-wide key-down tap is a keylogger with a different name. The defence that holds is
that a key code never leaves `tap.py` for anything but a comparison: nothing writes one to a
log, a file, or the archive, and the module says so in as many words.

And the audio only ever goes to a process stt started. The port for each model is chosen by
binding a socket, reading the number and closing it, because `whisper-server` has no "pick
one and tell me" mode — so after it answers, stt asks the operating system who owns that
listening socket and refuses to send anything if the answer is not its own child. Without
that, a local process which grabbed the port in the gap and replied to a health check would
have been handed every recorded sentence.

## What the gate is for, and what it cost to get right

A Whisper model handed audio with no speech in it does not stay quiet, it invents. In a file
that is a line to delete afterwards; here it is typed into somebody's window while nobody is
speaking. Both of these happened during development: two seconds of digital silence came
back as "Продолжение следует...", and a real run in a quiet room put "Thank you." into a
TextEdit document because one noise held the gate open for eighty milliseconds.

So the gate is tuned against recordings of this machine's own microphone rather than
guessed at:

| | median RMS | p90 | transients |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| eight seconds of a quiet room | 16 | 30 | to 1014 |
| speech at arm's length | 4550 | 6755 | — |

The threshold now sits an order of magnitude above the room and an order of magnitude below
a voice, and an utterance has to contain a third of a second of loud audio in total before
it counts as one — longer than any click, shorter than any word. The room recording produces
no utterance at all; the speech recording still produces exactly one.

## Two things measured and then deliberately not built

**`audio_ctx`** shortens whisper's fixed thirty-second encoder window and looks like free
latency. On a three-second window it made `large-v3-turbo` four times *slower*, and `base`
was already at forty milliseconds.

**`no_speech_prob`** is the model's own answer to "was anybody speaking", and would have
been the evidence for dropping an ordinary-sounding phrase without swallowing somebody who
genuinely said it. Asked about eight seconds of room noise it answered 0.000 while inventing
"Спасибо." out of it.

Both are recorded as comments where somebody would otherwise reach for them again.

## Ending, and not ending by accident

Two presses of Escape finish the session, and so does Ctrl-C — handled on the event loop
rather than left to raise, so the last sentence still settles and the transcript still
prints instead of being discarded along with the models.

A second `stt mic` refuses to start while one is running, and refuses *before* loading a
model rather than after: two sessions type into the same window and each deletes what it
believes it wrote, which is by then interleaved with the other's. The result is not two
transcripts, it is one line of debris, and neither session can tell anything is wrong.

A session nobody has spoken into for half an hour ends on its own. A microphone left open is
a room being recorded and a window that gets typed into by whoever speaks near the machine
next; nobody chooses that, they walk away from the terminal. The clicks an empty room makes
do not count as somebody speaking, or a forgotten session would never time out in the one
place it most needs to.

## What it deliberately does not have

**No menu bar icon.** That needs an `NSApplication` event loop running inside the process,
which is a lot of machinery for a small thing. The notifications turned out to be nearly
free after all — `osascript` ships on every Mac and shows a banner without a bundle of our
own, at the cost of the banner being attributed to Script Editor. So the state is reported in
three places that cost nothing: a live status line in the terminal, a short system sound as
the microphone opens and closes, and a banner for each of those two moments. `-q` turns all
three off.

**No underline under provisional text**, the way Apple's own dictation marks what it has not
decided yet. Marked text is drawn by the receiving application's text system and only an
input method can ask for it; an input method is a separate installed application, not a
command. `--no-draft` types nothing until it is final, for anyone who would rather never see
a wrong word.

## What review changed

Three rounds, and the findings worth naming were all about the same promise — that stt never
touches text it does not own:

- Ownership was a single flag. Take over sentence A, start sentence B before A has decoded,
  and beginning B cleared the flag; A's answer then arrived and was typed at whatever caret
  you had moved to. It is remembered per sentence now.
- The interrupt was handed to the event loop with `call_soon_threadsafe`, which reads as the
  careful thing to do and was the wrong thing: the loop is what performs the edits, so a
  click arriving while it was already about to type left the edit ahead of the interrupt in
  the queue. It happens on the tap's own thread now — three attribute writes, nothing to
  wake up.
- A sentence the typist declined was still recorded, so the printed transcript could disagree
  with the window about what had happened.
- A keyboard watcher that never finished starting looked like success, and dictation would
  have begun with nothing watching for your keystrokes at all.
- `_settle_each` promises nothing raises out of it and caught only diagnosed errors; with two
  sentences queued, anything else killed the consumer and hung the session.
- The readiness probe accepted any HTTP responder on the port, and `stt mic` ignored a
  configured `whispercpp_root` that file transcription honours.
- The gate learned its noise floor from speech frames as well as silence, so the floor
  climbed about four percent a second through a long sentence until the sentence stopped
  clearing its own threshold. A steady quiet voice was cut off after thirteen seconds and
  every second after that raised the floor further, so the rest of what they said never
  reached a model at all. The floor is a model of the room, and while somebody is talking
  you are not observing the room — it only adapts between utterances now. The comment that
  used to sit there said this could not happen because the climb was slow; slow is not the
  same as bounded.
- `stt mic` ignored `dictionary` and `dict_bias`, which the file pipeline honours, so
  somebody who had turned the dictionary off to keep the spelling they dictated was having
  it corrected anyway — and their glossary sent to the models on top. It ignored the user's
  own `hallucinations.txt` for the same reason.
- A draft that nothing replaced was abandoned rather than removed. A cough gets through the
  gate, the fast model hears an ordinary word in it, and the accurate model answers with
  something the filters drop — the draft then stayed on screen for good, because settling
  forgot stt owned it and no later edit could reach it. That is stt typing a word nobody
  said into somebody's window and walking away from it, which is precisely what the
  "deletes only what it typed" invariant is supposed to make impossible.
- A keyboard watcher that timed out during startup was reported as failed and left running:
  the thread was only late, not dead, so it could reach its run loop a moment afterwards and
  then watch every key for the life of the process with nobody holding a reference to switch
  it off. A system-wide watcher that nothing owns is the last thing to leave behind.
- Backspaces were counted in code points, and a macOS text field deletes what a reader calls
  one character. Revising text that ended in "é" written as e-plus-accent, or a family emoji
  written as four people joined by zero-width joiners, asked for seven backspaces where the
  field needed one — and the other six came out of whatever the user had written before stt
  started typing. They are counted in grapheme clusters now, conservatively: where the rule
  is wrong it under-counts, which leaves a few of stt's own characters behind rather than
  taking any of the user's. Pairing flag emoji by looking back two code points was then
  wrong for two adjacent flags — the fourth regional indicator decided it was starting a
  fresh one, making a pair count as three — so they are counted by parity across the whole
  run. (The cluster rule itself is unit-tested but has not yet been watched in a live window
  — see the note in `typist.py`.)
- `--idle-minutes -1` parsed, became zero, and switched the timeout off. Zero does mean
  "never", but nobody types a minus sign to ask for that, and a typo left the microphone
  open indefinitely — the one outcome the timeout exists to prevent. `nan` did it more
  quietly still, since every comparison against it is false. Both are refused now.
- The draft's `_put` sat outside its own exception guard, so a refused keystroke or a bad
  dictionary term killed the task with nobody to receive the exception — and the next tick
  started another draft that failed identically, once a second, for the rest of the session.
- Confirming the port belongs to our own child is done before every decode rather than once
  at startup. It was assumed to be too expensive for that, and then measured: nine
  milliseconds, against forty for a draft answer. An assumption about cost is not a reason to
  send somebody's voice to a process that might not be the one stt started.
- `stt doctor` looked for `whisper-server` only on PATH while `stt mic` honours the
  configured checkout, so somebody who had installed whisper.cpp where they told stt about it
  was shown "NOT found" and an install instruction for something they already had.
- The claim that the cluster counting was "safe because it under-counts" turned out to be
  false for scripts nobody here had tried. `क्ष` is one character in a text field and was
  counted as two, because the consonant after the virama looked like a fresh start — and the
  second backspace comes out of whatever was in front of stt's text. Hangul written as
  separate jamo had the same problem. Every rule in that function now only ever says "these
  two are one character", never the reverse, so being wrong can only leave stt's own
  characters behind.
- The flagship failure had a second way in. A click clears the gate's onset, the fast model
  hears an ordinary word in it and types that word — and then the gate throws the utterance
  away for holding no real speech, so no accurate pass ever runs and nothing was left to take
  the word back. The gate reports a discarded utterance now, and the guess is removed.
- A sentence rewrite is a couple of hundred backspaces, posted in one burst. A click landing
  after the first of them was answered by posting the rest anyway, deleting whatever the user
  had just typed at their new caret. Ownership is asked about between every keystroke.
- Checking who owns the model's port before every decode narrowed that race and did not close
  it — there is still a gap between the answer and the send. What closes it is that a TCP
  connection, once established, cannot be handed to anybody else: the connection is opened
  once, checked at that moment, and kept. It is also faster, at 47 ms a decode against 67.
- The HTTP status of the model's reply was ignored. A refusal comes back as a JSON object
  with an `error` key and no `text`, and reading only `text` turned that into an empty answer
  — indistinguishable from "the model heard nothing", so dictation removed every draft and
  typed nothing for a whole session with no reason given anywhere.
- A fatal decode failure recorded itself and let the queue carry on. Every sentence spoken
  while the failing one was decoding was still sent to a model that had just proved it does
  not answer, each able to wait out the ninety-second timeout in turn, with the microphone
  open throughout — and a sentence decoded after the error could still be typed.
- `stt mic` refused to start at all when the small draft model was not on disk. `stt setup`
  downloads the one model it was asked for, so anybody who accepted the default had
  `large-v3-turbo` and no `base` — and the first `stt mic` they ever ran failed before opening
  the microphone, over a model nobody had told them they needed. The fast pass is a
  convenience; it now says so and dictates without it.
- The kept connection was never re-established. `http.client` does not reconnect by itself,
  so a server tidying up an idle connection between two sentences — an ordinary thing to do —
  made the next request fail, and that failure ended the session. One retry, and only for a
  broken connection: a refusal would be the same refusal however many times it is asked.
- The replacement text was posted in bursts with the ownership check only in front of the
  first, so a click after that burst was answered by posting the rest into the newly focused
  window. It is asked about between every piece, and the pieces never split a character.
- Only left-clicks were watched, so a right-click or an extra mouse button moved the caret to
  another window without stt noticing — and the next correction went wherever the click had
  landed.
- Cancelling a draft does not stop the worker thread already inside the request, so a
  cancelled draft could still be using the connection when the next one started. Two requests
  on one `HTTPConnection` is not something it supports: the replies come back interleaved, or
  matched to the wrong question. Actual use of the connection is serialised in the threads.
- The idle timer only reset when an utterance CLOSED, and the gate holds one open until a
  pause or twenty-five seconds — so a short `--idle-minutes` and one long sentence ended the
  session mid-word, which is the opposite of what "nobody has spoken" means.
- A `--draft-model` that is not a model at all was swallowed as "no fast guess", and the note
  told the user to run `stt models pull definitely-not-a-model` — worse than saying nothing,
  because it reads like the answer. Only a model that exists and is not downloaded is
  downgraded now.
- The configured `threads` was ignored and `-t 0` became four, so somebody who had set eight
  got four and somebody asking for the engine default got four as well, with two servers
  between them oversubscribing the machine. Zero keeps the meaning it has everywhere else.
- A connection cancelled while it was still being made leaked its socket, and two drafts
  arriving together could each build one and leave the loser's open. Closed on any exit,
  cancellation included, and only one is ever built at a time.
- A stale request failing late closed whichever connection was current, which by then could
  be the healthy replacement — cutting off the retry that was working and stopping drafting
  for the rest of the session. The caller says which connection it was holding, and only that
  one is dropped.
- `show()` restored its idea of the line after the keystrokes, and `disown()` runs on the
  watcher's thread and can land between them. The typist then went on believing it owned
  characters at a caret the user had since moved, and the correction after the next sentence
  backspaced over whatever was now in front of it. Ownership is asked about again after the
  keystrokes, and losing it mid-edit leaves the text alone for good.
- Clearing the "a sentence is settling" flag between one queued sentence and the next left a
  gap wide enough to draft in. Sentence A is slow, B queues behind it, A returns — and before
  B starts, the user's sentence C is drafted and typed, after which B comes back and rewrites
  C's draft into B's older words.
- The port ownership check was done once at startup, and it expires the moment the process
  behind it exits — the port is free again, and the next sentence would go to whatever bound
  it. Each decode now confirms the child is still alive first.

Each has a test that was checked by removing the fix and watching it fail. Three of those
tests initially passed with their own fix removed — asserting something true either way — and
were rewritten to assert what actually differs. A test that cannot fail is worse than no test,
because it retires the question.

One finding was declined. Clicking into another window and then speaking types the sentence
there, which was reported as "text goes to the newly focused app despite the click" — but the
click is how you choose where to dictate, and refusing on those grounds would break the
ordinary way anybody uses this. What the click protects is the sentence already on screen
when it happened, and that one is never touched again. Both halves are now pinned by tests so
neither gets "fixed" into the other.

## The silent failure, and the command that ends it

The last rounds were spent on one class of defect rather than on the concurrency: **`stt mic`
could do nothing at all and say nothing about it.** No text, no error, no exit code. Four
different causes produced that same silence, and from outside they were indistinguishable —
a denied Microphone permission, the wrong device open, a room too loud for the threshold, and
nobody having actually spoken. Diagnosing it once took four throwaway scripts and most of a
session to arrive at a single number: the loudest thing heard was 454 and the detector wanted
1500.

Four fixes came out of that, each with a test verified by removing the fix:

- **The bar was six times its documented value.** One constant did two jobs — the clamp that
  keeps the learned noise floor off exact zero, and the absolute bar a frame must clear. The
  floor was clamped at 250, the bar is the floor times six, so the smallest bar the detector
  could ever set was 1500 while its own comment called 250 the minimum. They are two constants
  now.
- **`stt mic --check` was two printed lines, one of which said "not checked here"** — about
  the permission people actually wanted to know about. It now opens the microphone, draws
  what it hears against the bar it has to clear, and names which of the four causes it was.
  It tells a voice from a keystroke by duration rather than level, and it measures against
  the same gate a session would build: a check that answers a slightly different question
  than the tool it diagnoses is worse than no check.
- **A microphone that died was reported as a clean finish.** ffmpeg's exit status was never
  examined, so a device unplugged mid-sentence read as the recording having ended normally.
- **`--device 5` opened a microphone called "EchoWhiskey536".** A number that matched no index
  fell through to substring matching on the names.

Level alone cannot separate a quiet voice from a loud room — measured here, a keystroke in a
silent room reaches 1014 and a voice a metre away reaches 812. So the bar is a choice, not a
constant: the default favours hearing the voice, and `mic_threshold` in the config buys the
other trade for a room where stray noises being typed costs more.

## Two checks that could be skipped, and so were not checks

- **The port ownership check had a fallback.** The model's port is chosen by binding a socket
  and closing it, so another local process can take it in the gap and be sent every recorded
  sentence along with the terminology prompt. `lsof` is what proves the listener is the
  process stt started — and the check was skipped when `lsof` was missing, on the reasoning
  that a utility should not stop a microphone from opening. That made the single defence
  removable by arranging for `lsof` not to be found. It refuses now; `lsof` ships with macOS
  and `stt mic` is macOS-only, so the refusal is theoretical in practice and total when it
  is not.
- **`mic_threshold` accepted `inf`.** Every real level compares false against it, so the
  setting switched the detector off in silence: microphone open, nothing typed, no error, and
  `--check` reporting a perfectly loud voice as too quiet. `--idle-minutes` had the identical
  hole and it was closed one setting at a time, which is exactly how the second one happened
  — so non-finite and negative values are now refused for every numeric setting at once.

## The activation sound, measured rather than chosen

macOS ships fourteen sounds and none of them says "the microphone is live". The cue is
generated instead, from `wave` and `math`: one pair of tones, rising for open and falling for
close, so the two need no learning. The numbers came from measuring a dictation cue people
already like. All four of the first attempt's were wrong the same way — an octave too high,
four times too loud, no decay at all, and more than twice too long.

The length error is worth keeping: the comparison used FILE length, and the reference is a
180 ms file holding 47 ms of sound. A listener heard the difference the measurement could not
show. The check now measures audible length, and pinning it caught a defect in the envelope
itself — the exponential decay was cut off at a tenth of full volume, which is a click, the
one artefact the envelope exists to prevent.

## How much review this had

Twenty-four rounds, two independent reviewers each round. The rounds that stopped finding
concurrency failures kept finding this other family, which is the more valuable half: a
deadlock announces itself, and a tool that quietly does nothing does not.

## Verified, not only unit-tested

- Russian text typed into a real TextEdit document, including a rewrite in place and an emoji
- the microphone read in real time through ffmpeg, at the correct rate
- a full pass from audio to typed text, through both real models
- a quiet room for forty seconds: nothing typed, empty transcript
- Ctrl-C finishes the session and prints the transcript instead of discarding it
- both models unloaded afterwards, no processes left behind, including when a server never
  became ready in the first place
- 120 requests in a row against one server, to prove the log pipe cannot wedge it
- an end-to-end run driven by a recording played into the microphone, typing Russian into a
  TextEdit document opened for the purpose — with a focus check that abandons the run rather
  than typing into whatever the user is actually looking at

Zero new dependencies: the four macOS calls are reached through `ctypes`, and the microphone
is opened with the ffmpeg stt already requires.

title: fix: diarization runs in a uv environment instead of installing into the system Python
body:
## What this fixes

`stt diarize install` could not work on a standard Homebrew setup:

```
error: The interpreter at /opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/... is externally managed
```

It ran pip against `sys.executable`, and Homebrew's interpreter is marked externally
managed, so PEP 668 refuses outright. The documented ways past that refusal exist to be
discouraged — they would put two and a half gigabytes of torch into an interpreter Homebrew
owns and rebuilds on its next upgrade.

## The fix was already in this repository

`backends/mlx.py` never installs anything. It runs its heavy dependency through
`uv run --with mlx-whisper python` in a worker subprocess, so uv builds and caches the
environment and nothing touches a Python the user did not create. Diarization now does the
same, through a new `diarize_worker.py` shaped exactly like `mlx_worker.py` — argv in, one
JSON object out.

So `stt diarize install` is no longer an install. It warms that cache, which means the
download happens once, visibly, when it was asked for, rather than inside somebody's first
transcription. Nothing is left to uninstall but a uv cache entry.

## Five defects the change itself introduced, and one it exposed

Each was found by review, and each has a test checked by removing the fix and watching it
fail.

- **The readiness check asked the wrong interpreter** (exposed, not introduced).
  `is_installed()` imported into ours, but the wheels live in uv's — so a machine perfectly
  able to diarize was told it could not.
- **Asking whether it was ready would have downloaded 2.5 GB.** A bare `uv run --with`
  resolves when the cache is cold, so `stt diarize status` — and `stt doctor`, which people
  run precisely when they want no surprises — would have fetched torch in order to answer a
  question. The probe is `--offline` now: a cached environment answers, a cold one fails, and
  failing is the honest "no".
- **The Hugging Face token went into argv.** Any user on the machine can read another
  process's arguments, and diarizing an hour of audio keeps that process alive for an hour.
  It travels in the environment now — the channel `huggingface_hub` reads anyway.
- **The status could raise.** It caught only diagnosed errors, so a timeout would have come
  out of `stt doctor` as the traceback that command exists to replace.
- **The result was read as the last line of stdout.** Anything torch or pyannote flushes on
  its way out would have discarded an hour of finished work. The reply is searched for now,
  not assumed to be in a particular place.
- **The timeout arrived with the subprocess and was not handled.** Moving work out of process
  gives it a deadline whether anybody wanted one or not, and a fixed hour was wrong at both
  ends — too long to notice a wedge on a two-minute memo, and short enough to cut off a
  three-hour recording that used to finish, because the in-process call had no limit at all.
  It scales with the audio now, and running out is a sentence rather than a stack trace.

## On the test that runs a real subprocess

The token test originally asserted on what was handed to a mocked `proc.run`. A reviewer
pointed out that this proves nothing about the subprocess: if `proc.run` replaced the
environment instead of merging it, the worker would run with no `HOME`, uv could not find its
cache, huggingface could not find `~/.cache/huggingface`, and the token would be delivered
perfectly to a process unable to use it — while status and doctor stayed green and only real
diarization broke. It now launches an actual subprocess and asserts that it sees both the
token and `HOME`.

## Verified

- `stt diarize status` reports `pyannote.audio: ready` on the machine where the install used
  to fail, and `stt doctor` shows a tick rather than a cross.
- 479 tests.

Closes #28.

title: fix: the top-level `stt --help` is coloured like every subcommand's
body:
Alex noticed that `stt --help` came out grey while `stt doctor --help` came out colourful. Both are the same program answering the same kind of question, so the difference read as a defect.

## Why it happened

Subcommand help is built by `argparse`, which paints its own output from Python 3.14 on. The top-level help is a hand-written string printed straight through `print()`, so nothing ever coloured it.

## What this does

It asks argparse for the palette it is about to use rather than inventing one. `palette.for_help()` reads CPython's own theme through CPython's own `can_colorize`, so the top level and its subcommands cannot disagree — on any Python version, in any terminal.

Where argparse leaves help plain (Python 3.11 and 3.13, a pipe, `NO_COLOR`, a dumb terminal) every field of the palette is the empty string, and the f-strings that embed them produce byte-for-byte the text they produced before. That equality is asserted by a test, not assumed.

Padding is measured on the text without escape sequences, so a coloured row lands in exactly the column a plain one did. The hand-aligned help lines became `(invocation, summary)` pairs rendered into a column, so the alignment cannot drift by hand again.

## The test that was not testing anything

The first `NO_COLOR` test was gated behind the real version probe, so on Python 3.11 and 3.13 — which is what CI runs — it returned before reaching the branch it claimed to cover. A regression that ignored `NO_COLOR` entirely would have gone green. It now stands in for CPython's private colour module so the branch executes on every version; removing the check under test makes it fail, which was verified rather than assumed.

## Checks

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy stt_cli` and 491 tests, each exit code read separately. Reviewed across two models with no findings.

title: fix: declare the version where the release tooling looks for it
body:
Every ship today needed a written override saying the release check was wrong about this project. It was — but a person who types that override monthly stops reading it, and then types it on the day the check is right.

## Why the check was wrong

The version lived in `stt_cli/__init__.py`, and `pyproject.toml` pointed back at it through a `version = { attr = ... }` indirection. That is tidy and it is unreadable to the gate, which opens pyproject looking for a number and finds a reference it cannot follow. A correctly bumped release reads as unbumped.

The number now lives in `pyproject.toml` and nowhere else. A test greps the package for a second literal, because two copies are exactly the problem being fixed.

## Reading it back is the interesting half

The obvious route — ask the installed metadata — was measured and rejected on two counts:

- **It costs about 20 ms** on every invocation, against an import-clean contract that promises `stt --help` is instant.
- **It lies.** This machine's metadata answered `0.1.0` while the source said `0.3.1`. An editable install records its version once and then keeps answering with it.

So a source checkout answers from `pyproject.toml` one directory up — 0.2 ms, and always the version of the tree in front of you. A real wheel, which ships no `pyproject.toml`, answers from its own metadata. That second path is the only one a released copy can take and the only one a checkout never exercises, so it has a test rather than only the manual check I did (build wheel → install into a clean environment → `stt --version` → `0.3.3`).

Resolution is lazy and cached: no command but `stt --version` pays for it, and a long-running process reading it twice does not open the file twice.

## What review caught, over six rounds

**A `pyproject.toml` that is not valid UTF-8 crashed `stt --version`.** `tomllib` decodes the bytes itself, so such a file fails before any TOML parsing does — a different exception than the one being caught, inside a function whose docstring promises it never raises.

**Any neighbouring `pyproject.toml` was trusted.** `pip install --target ./app` drops the package beside the host application's project file, and `stt --version` would have reported *that application's* version. It is the same mistake `uv run` makes without `--no-project`, one directory up. Now guarded by the project name.

**The laziness test was empty.** Patching a function proves nothing once the module holding it has been imported, so the test passed against the very change it existed to catch. It now asks a fresh interpreter whether the TOML parser was loaded.

**The distribution name was written twice** — in a change whose entire point is that one number should be written once.

**And the wheel-path test would have failed rather than skipped on a bare clone**, quietly raising the bar for the whole suite when every other test here needs only an importable package.

Each fix was verified by removing it and watching the test go red.

## Checks

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy stt_cli` and 493 tests, each exit code read separately. Six review rounds across two models; the last came back clean.

title: dev shot: capture-measure-attest visual proof that cannot be faked
body:
Closes #4

## The problem

The `visual-proof-gate` accepted **any file with a recent mtime** in `~/.cache/agent-tools/visual-proof/`. A bare `touch` satisfied it, so the attestation carried no information:

- an agent that never opened a browser could pass it;
- an agent that captured a **blank page** could pass it just as easily.

Both happened in one project. A capture that was attested on in good faith turned out to be **52% featureless rows with a single 2,773px blank band** — 42% of the page — because reveal-on-scroll sections were photographed while still at `opacity: 0`. The mismatch numbers computed from it were measured largely against blank page.

## The approach

`dev shot` takes the caller out of the attesting path. It performs the capture, judges it, and writes the record itself.

```bash
dev shot http://localhost:4173/ --out shot.png --viewport 1440x900
```

1. **The tool captures** — viewport set *before* `open` (agent-browser silently ignores `open --width`), then a scroll sweep sized to the real `scrollHeight` so reveal-gated content has entered the viewport before the shutter.
2. **The tool judges** — a degenerate capture is rejected before any record exists. Primary check is the largest *contiguous* blank band, not the uniform-row count.
3. **The record is bound to the work** — capture sha256 + `git diff --cached` sha256.

## Why the band metric

Grounded in two real captures of the same page, committed as fixtures:

| | uniform rows | largest band |
|---|---|---|
| unswept (bad) | 52.4% | **42.3%** |
| swept (good) | 19.5% | **4.2%** |

Uniform-row count separates them only 2.7x and misfires on ordinary page whitespace. The largest contiguous band separates them **10x**. Threshold is 15%, leaving >2x headroom on both sides — asserted by a test so a future loosening can't pass quietly.

## Hardening (six review rounds)

- Empty staged diff counts as **unbound** — `git commit -am` stages *after* the gate runs, so an empty-diff hash would otherwise match anything.
- Capture height checked against `scrollHeight` — closes the quietest false attestation: a clean viewport-only shot of a tall page has no blank band and the right width, but omits most of the page.
- Measurement and hashing share **one read**, so a concurrent writer can't swap the bytes in between.
- `write_attestation` takes a `Verdict` and refuses a failed one — the invariant is structural, not a docstring plea.
- Inflated IDAT bounded against the declared scanline size (small-header decompression bomb); viewport refused before the backend allocates.
- Decode and filesystem errors normalised to `CaptureError`; exit **4** for binding failures a retake cannot fix.
- Recorded URL read back from the browser, left **unknown** rather than assumed when unreadable.
- `worktree_dirty` recorded, so the index-vs-worktree gap is visible to the gate.
- All five PNG filter types pinned by test — a wrong unfilter fails *open*.

## Residual trust (stated plainly)

This is process discipline, **not** a security boundary. An agent with shell access can still write a record directly. What it does prevent is the *good-faith* failure that actually occurs: attesting to a capture nobody looked at, or one that is mostly blank.

Known gaps, deliberately not closed here: the binding is to the index while the pixels come from the working tree (now flagged via `worktree_dirty`); `--out` isn't project-scoped like other path arguments; and the shared agent-browser session has a residual race that degrades to a rejection rather than a false record.

## Verification

- 173 tests pass, `ruff` clean.
- End-to-end against a live site: 1440x6036 captured, band 4.4%, record written with both hashes bound.
- Both real fixtures assert the intended verdict.

Requires the companion gate change in `agent-tools` to verify the binding.

title: fix(stop): confirm pid/port death before reporting dev stop success (#27)
body:
## Summary

Fixes the stop-race in dev-cli#27: `dev stop` could report success and remove the state
record while the target process was still alive (SIGTERM ignored, or the process just
hadn't been reaped yet), and `dev status`/`dev list` could misreport a port as free when
an unmanaged process or a forked child had inherited the listening socket.

## Acceptance criteria (from #27)

- [x] **`dev stop` blocks until the pid (or process group) is confirmed dead before
  unlinking state / printing success, escalating to SIGKILL on a timeout.**
  Implemented via `_wait_until_dead`/`_wait_until_group_dead` (5s grace, 50ms poll) called
  from `_terminate_pid`/`_stop_process_group`, escalating through
  `_send_signal_best_effort`/`_send_process_group_signal_best_effort`.
  Proof:
  - `test_terminate_pid_escalates_to_sigkill_when_grace_expires` (mocked clock, no real
    sleep) — asserts `sent == [SIGTERM, SIGKILL]` once the grace window expires.
  - `test_stop_target_kills_child_that_ignores_sigterm_before_removing_state` — spawns a
    **real subprocess** that installs `SIG_IGN` for SIGTERM, asserts the state record is
    NOT removed while the child is confirmed alive, and IS removed only after the SIGKILL
    escalation actually kills it.

- [x] **`dev status`/`dev list` never read a target as flat "stale"/"configured" when
  something is still listening on its port** (unmanaged process, or a forked child that
  inherited the listening socket after the tracked pid died).
  Implemented via `_port_occupied` (TCP connect probe to 127.0.0.1 then `::1`) feeding new
  `_record_state`/`_configured_state` helpers, adding two states: `"stale (port busy)"` and
  `"running (unmanaged)"`.
  Proof:
  - `test_status_probes_port_for_unmanaged_listener_with_no_state_record` — no state
    record, real listener bound on the target's configured port -> reports
    `running (unmanaged)`.
  - `test_status_probes_port_after_stale_pid` — dead tracked pid, real listener still on
    the recorded port -> reports `stale (port busy)` instead of a bare `stale`.
  - `test_port_occupied_false_for_closed_port` — closed port probes false (no
    false-positive "busy" reporting).

- [x] **Existing stop/pgid regression coverage stays accurate under the new
  confirmed-dead contract.** ~8 pre-existing tests updated so their `_pid_alive`/
  `_process_group_members` mocks reflect the process/group actually dying after the
  signal is sent (otherwise the new poll loop spins the full grace window and wrongly
  fires a SIGKILL, breaking `sent == [...]` assertions). Full scoped run:
  `python -m pytest tests/test_dev_cli.py -q` -> **120 passed**.

## Notes

- Ruff clean on both changed files (`ruff check dev_cli/cli.py tests/test_dev_cli.py`).
- Fixed a startup race discovered while verifying the new real-subprocess test: the child
  script now prints `ready` immediately after installing `SIG_IGN`, and the test blocks on
  that line before triggering `dev stop`, so the SIGTERM can never race the child's own
  startup and kill it via the default disposition before the ignore handler is installed.
  Verified stable across 5 repeated runs of the affected tests.

Refs #27

title: feat(pm): pm-reminders-push cron wrapper for stuck-task Telegram digests
body:
Closes #2.

## What
`bin/pm-reminders-push` — cron-driven shim: runs the hyperide task-cli ingest, computes `pm reminders`, and pushes ONE Telegram digest via `tg` when reminders are non-empty. Silent exit 0 on an empty set (no all-clear spam, 3x/day unattended). An ERR trap logs locally and sends a distinct failure ping so a broken pipeline can't impersonate a quiet one.

Crontab entry (installed on the target machine, not in-repo):
`47 8,14,19 * * * /Users/ultra/xp/pm-cli/bin/pm-reminders-push >> /Users/ultra/.local/state/pm/reminders-push.log 2>&1`

## Hardening (6 review-cli iterations, findings fixed)
- explicit cron PATH — `task`, Homebrew python3 (pm needs >=3.11, /usr/bin/python3 is 3.9), bun (tg shebang), jq are all transitive deps of a bare-PATH cron run
- tg enrichment disabled on every send (`--no-feature auto-attach/autolink-tasks/autolink-msgrefs`): reminder text quoting a file path must not upload it; no per-item linear lookups
- ERR trap armed before log setup; script owns its log (`exec >> $LOG`) so the failure ping's pointer is always true
- null-aware contract guard on `pm reminders --json` (fail-loud on shape drift — deliberate, documented)
- one-reminder-one-line invariant: whole-line whitespace folding incl. VT/FF/NEL/U+2028/U+2029
- 120-char raw detail budget for Telegram's 4096 limit; `'` → `'` (jq 1.7 emits `'`, Telegram basic HTML lacks it — verified empirically)
- strict `MAX_ITEMS` validation (0 / 007 / 08 octal traps fall back to 10)
- `PM_PUSH_DRY_RUN=1` render-only preview (skips ingest, prints via saved fd3, no Telegram)

## Verification (all under `env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin` cron simulation)
- happy path: silent exit 0, empty log
- forced ingest failure: timestamped log line + fake-tg called with exactly `--tag problem --no-feature ...`
- unwritable $LOG: trap still pings
- render pipeline: 12-item overflow caps at 10 + footer; exotic separators fold to one line; entities correct

## Out-of-scope P1s found by review, filed
- #3 ingest never refreshes tracked ticket state (stale reminders — known limitation until fixed)
- #4 degraded project fetches dropped silently (needs strict ingest mode)
- #5 move digest rendering + tests into pm itself

title: fix(reconcile): discover PR urls via task-cli attachments
body:
## Summary

`pm reconcile --source pr` always returned `scanned:0` — for every ticket, forever. `pr_url_for(item)` only reads `pr` evidence already recorded on the item, and nothing ever wrote that evidence: `pm ingest --source task` records only `task-record` evidence (the ticket's own url), because `task list --json` (what bulk ingest calls) omits the `attachments` field where a ticket's linked GitHub PR url actually lives. Only `task read <id> --json` carries it, per-ticket. Verified against real task-cli output shapes (`task read HYP-1256 --json`) against the hyperide repo.

- `pmlib/adapters/task.py` gets `extract_pr_url` (pure) and `fetch_ticket_attachments` (effectful, `task read <id> --json`) as a second pure/effectful pair alongside the existing bulk-ingest one.
- `pmlib/commands/reconcile.py`'s new `_discover_pr_urls` shells this for any item still missing `pr` evidence and feeds the result into `fetch_pr_facts`'s new `discovered_urls` fallback parameter. This runs at **reconcile time**, not ingest time, so it backfills items ingested before this fix existed too — the actual bug closed here — not just future ones.

Hardened across 5 review rounds (2 Opus correctness passes clean, several GLM performance/quality passes):
- Tries every `task_ref` on an item, not just the first (an item can aggregate multiple tracked tickets).
- A missing `task` binary / bad `--repo-dir` degrades discovery only, instead of aborting the whole reconcile run (a real regression caught in round 2 — the first version let the error propagate and killed items that never needed `task` at all).
- `gh pr view` and `task read` results are memoized per-URL/per-ticket within a run.
- Both new subprocess calls get a 30s timeout so a hung backend can't stall the whole run.
- The PR-url regex tolerates a query string/fragment tail without leaking it into the returned canonical url.
- `fetch_pr_facts` returns a copy of each memoized fact dict, not a shared object.
- A bad `--repo-dir` no longer misreports as "task not found".

**Deliberately deferred, documented in the module docstring:** single `--repo-dir` assumes a single task-cli project (same scope `pm ingest` already has); no negative caching for tickets confirmed to have no PR (re-probed every run — acceptable at the measured ~100-ticket scale); no parallelization of the subprocess calls.

Ticket: https://github.com/alex-mextner/pm-cli/issues/11

## Test plan
- [x] `python3 -m pytest tests/` — 212 passed (1 pre-existing, unrelated failure: `test_monthly_report_groups_product_and_process`, a date-sensitive test broken by clock drift, fails identically on clean `main`)
- [x] `python3 -m ruff check .` — clean
- [x] Regression tests use the REAL `attachments` payload captured from `task read HYP-1256 --json` (hyperide/hyper-ext-e2e#155): discovery → gh facts → state advance, convergence (discovered urls aren't re-probed once real `pr` evidence lands), the already-has-pr-evidence skip path, the missing-task degrade path, and multi-ref/shared-ticket/shared-PR memoization.
- [x] Ran `pm ingest --source task --repo-dir /Users/ultra/work/hyperide` and `pm reconcile --source pr` for real against the hyperide backlog (results reported separately in Telegram)

title: feat(pm): sprint system (create/plan/start/status/close/retro) + architecture docs
body:
## Summary

Closes #35, #36.

- **Sprint system** (`pmlib/sprint.py` + `pm sprint` CLI): `create`/`add`/`start`/`status`/`close`/`retro`/`list`, event-sourced on the SAME append-only log pattern as everything else in pm (a second, independent pure fold — sprint and WorkItem events are mutually invisible, tested in both directions). `status`/`retro` always join LIVE against the WorkItem projection so a sprint's view of "done" can never drift.
- **"Autonomous" scoped to pm's Release-1 observe-only boundary**: 3 new sprint-lifecycle reminders (`sprint-stale-planning`, `sprint-ready-to-close`, `sprint-needs-retro`) wired into the existing `pm reminders` / `pm-reminders-push` cron surface — no new dispatch machinery, matching pm's own "observes and reconciles, does not dispatch" design rule.
- **`docs/architecture.md`**: a from-scratch write-up of how pm-cli is actually built (event-sourcing invariant, component map, the FSM, sprints, and the two concrete failure modes that motivated the whole tool), with 3 Mermaid diagrams.

## Process

4 rounds of this repo's multi-model review gate. Real bugs caught and fixed each round:
- Round 1: initial implementation.
- Round 2: `sprint-ready-to-close` false-positive on missing items (vacuous `all()`), malformed/non-finite estimate write+replay safety, `close`-from-`planning` guarded at both CLI and fold layers, `pm reminders`' single-read-then-fold-twice perf fix.
- Round 3: whitespace-only retro note silently satisfying the needs-retro nudge (both CLI and fold), doc-wording fix for `sprint-stale-planning`'s real (activity-based, not creation-based) semantics.
- Round 4 (performance + correctness pass): converged clean — *"Net: solid, ship-worthy."*

Deferred architectural + minor performance suggestions (lifecycle-rule duplication between the CLI and the fold, a `Sprint.errors` field mirroring `WorkItem.errors`, a library-level `compute_all_reminders` aggregator, quadratic replay cost at large re-add counts) tracked in #14 — none are correctness bugs, all are legitimate follow-up scope.

Also found and filed #13 (a pre-existing time-bomb test unrelated to this change — hardcodes month `2026-07` against `new_event()`'s real wall-clock timestamp).

## Test plan

- [x] `ruff check .` — clean
- [x] `python -m pytest -q` — 222 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure (#13), 40 new tests across 3 new test files
- [x] 4 rounds of multi-model review, all real findings fixed

title: feat(pm): sprint system (create/plan/start/status/close/retro) (#35, #36)
body:
## Summary
Supersedes #15 (same base content, now hardened across 13 review-cli rounds — see below). #15's branch had been stale/unpushed-to for a while, so this lands as a fresh branch rather than force-pushing over it.

- `pmlib/sprint.py` — pure event-fold projection for sprints (create/plan/start/status/close/retro)
- `pmlib/commands/sprint.py` — the CLI
- `docs/architecture.md` — architecture write-up with a corrected state diagram

## Hardening (all found + fixed via review-cli, 13 rounds)
- `EventStore.lock()` (cross-platform: fcntl on POSIX, msvcrt on Windows) serializes every sprint-mutating command's read-validate-append sequence — closes a real race where two concurrent commands (e.g. `add` + `start`) could both report success while one's event got silently discarded.
- The fold rejects malformed/foreign log input defensively: empty/non-string ids, null retro text, negative/boolean/oversized estimates, an aggregate total that would overflow to `inf`, and a `SPRINT_STARTED` for an empty sprint.
- Shared `display_safe()` helper (`pmlib/commands/_shared.py`) escapes ASCII C0 + DEL + Unicode C1 control chars — applied to every terminal-rendered log-sourced field across `sprint.py` and `reminders.py`, closing a real terminal escape-sequence (OSC/ANSI) injection path.
- `store.py`'s `read_all()` now tolerates a `TypeError` from a wrong-shaped field the same way it already tolerated torn/malformed JSON.

## Follow-ups filed (deliberately out of scope here)
- rig-cli TaskList #86: `commands/record.py`'s transition path has the same race this PR fixed for sprints, not yet migrated to `lock()`.
- rig-cli TaskList #87: broader terminal-escape sanitization sweep across the rest of pm-cli (queue, report, route, etc.).

## Test plan
- [x] `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` — 243 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure (confirmed present on plain `origin/main` too, `test_reports.py::test_monthly_report_groups_product_and_process`)
- [x] `ruff check pmlib/ tests/` — clean
- [x] `review diff --staged -C . --preset light --task 35` — CLEAN after 13 rounds

Closes rig-cli TaskList #35/#36.
